title: AI Systems and Useful Work
summary: Recognize what an AI system is, where it can help, and where human judgment remains essential.
objectives: Distinguish artificial intelligence, machine learning, models, and complete AI systems.
Match common AI capabilities to suitable tasks.
Identify the people, data, software, and controls surrounding a model.
Decide when an AI-assisted task needs human review or should not be automated.

sections.title: An AI product is a system, not a magic answer box
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence is a broad term for computer systems that perform tasks associated with perception, prediction, language, planning, or decision support. Machine learning is one way to create AI behavior by learning patterns from examples instead of writing every rule by hand.
A model is only one component. A useful AI system also includes instructions, input data, software, tools, permissions, user experience, monitoring, and people who remain accountable for the outcome.
When evaluating a product, ask what model or method it uses, what information it receives, what actions it can take, and what surrounding controls verify or limit its behavior.
sections.callout: Judge the whole system—including data, tools, people, and controls—not only the model response.

sections.title: Capability patterns help you find appropriate work
paragraphs: Generative systems are often useful for drafting, summarizing, explaining, transforming formats, extracting structure, classifying examples, brainstorming alternatives, and reasoning over material supplied in context.

Other AI systems may rank, recommend, detect patterns, forecast values, transcribe audio, interpret images, or control a physical process. The label AI does not tell you which capability is present or how reliable it is.
A good use case has a clear outcome, suitable data, a way to evaluate quality, and consequences that match the available controls.

sections.title: Assistance and automation are different decisions
paragraphs: An assistant proposes work for a person to inspect. An automated system may act without reviewing every output. The same model can create very different risk depending on whether it drafts a private outline or sends messages, changes records, or controls infrastructure.

Begin with assistance when the task is unfamiliar, evidence is incomplete, or mistakes are costly. Increase automation only after evaluation shows dependable behavior and the surrounding system can limit, observe, and reverse actions.
sections.callout: The right question is not only “Can AI do this?” but “Can this complete system do it safely enough for these consequences?”

sections.title: Human accountability does not disappear
paragraphs: People choose the objective, acceptable risk, data, model, tools, evaluation method, and response when something goes wrong. An AI output can inform a decision, but it cannot accept responsibility for the decision.
High-impact uses need clear ownership, documented review, accessible appeal or correction paths, and evidence that the system performs acceptably for the people and situations it affects.

sections.title: Four concrete cases for system-level triage
paragraphs: The following fictional dossier is a completed example, not a worksheet. Each case names the actual input or artifact, the objective, the capability, the affected people, the consequence of error, and the controls that surround the model.

Case one, library event description. Input: a librarian supplies a two-page event brief as a text document. Objective: produce three short announcements in plain language. Capability: generative text transformation and drafting. People: the librarian, event attendees, and the community organization hosting the event. Consequence: a wrong date, location, or accessibility detail could cause missed attendance or exclusion, but the draft can be corrected before publication. Permissions: the system can read the supplied brief and create a private draft, but it cannot publish or contact attendees. Reversibility: the draft can be discarded or edited. Monitoring: the librarian checks every date, name, link, and accessibility statement against the brief. Triage: AI assistance with review. Verification: compare each factual field with the source brief and have the event owner approve the final text. Stop condition: stop using the draft if it adds an event detail not present in the brief or if any required field cannot be verified.

Case two, food-pantry intake sorting. Inputs: a scanned intake form, a typed household size, a requested pickup date, and a list of available appointment slots. Objective: suggest a provisional appointment slot and identify missing fields for staff follow-up. Capability: document extraction, classification, and ranking. People: applicants, pantry staff, interpreters, and household members who may have limited access to food. Consequence: a mistaken suggestion could delay food access or expose sensitive information. Permissions: the system may read only the submitted form and available slots; it may draft a staff task but may not deny service, alter an applicant record, or send a message. Reversibility: staff can change or delete the suggestion before any contact. Monitoring: staff review every suggestion, sample records for missed fields, and record corrections by language and form type. Triage: AI assistance with review. Verification: staff confirm the household size, requested date, and eligibility-relevant fields against the original form. Stop condition: stop the classifier for a form type when staff find a repeated extraction error, an unreadable scan, or a pattern of missed fields for a language group.

Case three, municipal pothole queue. Inputs: geotagged photographs from residents, a location, a short description, and the existing road-maintenance queue. Objective: rank reports for inspection by combining visible severity and proximity to a school or transit stop. Capability: image interpretation, classification, and ranking. People: residents, pedestrians, cyclists, drivers, road crews, and people using nearby schools or transit. Consequence: a wrong rank may delay repair or misdirect a crew, but an inspector still makes the repair decision. Permissions: the system may add a proposed priority label to a separate review queue; it may not close a report, dispatch a crew, or change the public record. Reversibility: an inspector can replace the label and preserve the original report. Monitoring: inspect a sample of high and low rankings, log disagreement, and check whether image quality or location affects results. Triage: limited automation with approval, because assigning a proposed queue priority can reduce administrative sorting work while an inspector must approve every dispatch decision. This label follows that specified action boundary, not queue entry alone. A queue proposal for the school case is assistance with review because the hazard decision and work-order approval remain with the supervisor, the evidence is incomplete, and a missed hazard can injure someone. Verification: compare the proposed rank with an inspector's assessment and check the image, location, and description. Stop condition: suspend ranking and return to manual sorting if photographs are missing, locations are unreliable, or disagreement exceeds the team's pre-set tolerance.

Case four, greenhouse irrigation control. Inputs: soil-moisture readings from sensors, a weather forecast, crop type, irrigation limits, and a manual override log. Objective: decide when to open irrigation valves to keep plants within a safe moisture range. Capability: forecasting and physical-process control. People: greenhouse workers, the farm operator, customers relying on the crop, and anyone affected by water use. Consequence: an incorrect action could damage crops, waste water, create unsafe conditions, or cause costly equipment problems. Permissions: the proposed schedule may be displayed to a worker, but the system may not open valves automatically during the first release. Reversibility: a worker can reject the schedule, close valves, and use a manual procedure. Monitoring: sensor health, moisture readings, valve state, forecast changes, alerts, and a human log are reviewed. Triage: AI assistance with review, not automation, because the evidence is incomplete and the physical consequences are significant. Verification: a worker checks sensor status, crop stage, weather, and the proposed schedule before each action. Stop condition: stop using the proposal when a sensor is offline, readings conflict, the forecast changes sharply, a valve fails to respond, or the moisture range leaves its approved bounds. These cases do not need one of each release mode. Their modes follow the evidence, permissions, reversibility, and consequences in each case.
sections.callout: A capability does not determine a release mode by itself. The same ranking or generation method can be acceptable for a reviewed suggestion and unacceptable for an unreviewed decision.

sections.title: Trace one case from model to accountable action
paragraphs: Trace the food-pantry case from beginning to end. Artificial intelligence is the broad category of computer systems performing tasks associated with perception, prediction, language, planning, or decision support. Machine learning is one way to create such behavior by learning patterns from examples rather than receiving every rule by hand. A model is the learned or programmed component that produces an extraction, classification, or ranking. The complete AI system is larger: it includes the intake form, scan process, instructions, model, application software, access permissions, staff interface, logs, review procedure, and accountable pantry owner.

The input is a scanned form and appointment data. The model may extract a household size and classify a missing field. The application then places a suggestion in a staff queue. It does not follow that a model output is a fact, and it does not follow that a suggestion is a decision. Staff compare the suggestion with the original form, correct it when needed, and decide what happens next. The owner is the pantry organization and its designated staff, not the model.

This trace also separates assistance from action. Assistance proposes a result for a person to inspect. Action changes a record, sends a message, denies access, dispatches a crew, or controls equipment. Here, the system has permission to propose a task but not to deny service or contact an applicant. That boundary limits harm. Because evidence can be incomplete, staff must be able to mark a scan unreadable, ask for clarification, and avoid treating a confident-looking extraction as verified.

Accountability requires more than a named operator. The process needs a correction path when a household's information is extracted incorrectly, an appeal or escalation path when a person believes the process treated them unfairly, and an audit trail showing the original form, suggestion, correction, and final staff decision. The owner must review whether errors cluster around language, handwriting, disability-related formats, or scan quality. A person affected by the outcome must have a practical way to request correction without being forced to argue with the model.

Accountability also requires a correction path, an escalation or appeal path where appropriate, and an audit trail showing the original form, suggestion, correction, and final staff decision. The owner should check whether errors cluster around language, handwriting, disability-related formats, or scan quality. NIST's Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework describes AI systems as sociotechnical systems, so data, tools, people, and controls must be judged together with the model. NIST's Generative AI Profile is a risk-management companion. It is not being used here as a general capability catalog or as proof that a particular capability is safe. Sources: https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-1 and https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1.
sections.callout: A model can produce an output. The surrounding system determines who can rely on it, who can correct it, and what happens when it is wrong.

sections.title: Practice: complete one supplied case before choosing your own
paragraphs: This is the supplied exercise onramp. It is a learner task, not a completed answer. Use the food-pantry intake case from the dossier. On paper or in a local document, write one record with these labels: objective, actual input or artifact, capability, affected people, consequence of error, permissions, reversibility, monitoring, release mode, verification, stop condition, accountable owner, and correction or appeal path.

For the objective, state what the system is supposed to help staff accomplish, not a vague goal such as use AI. For the input, name the scanned form, typed household size, requested pickup date, and available appointment slots. For the capability, choose extraction, classification, ranking, generation, or another precise description. For the consequence, describe what a person could experience if the result is wrong.

Choose among no AI, AI assistance with review, limited automation with approval, and automation with monitoring. No AI is a valid choice when the task has no demonstrated benefit from AI, when a manual baseline is preferable, or when the proposed system lacks justification. Do not assume AI must be adopted. State what staff verify and the observable condition that stops the process. Identify who owns the decision and how an applicant can request correction. Do not write code. This exercise can be completed offline.
sections.callout: Complete this supplied case first. Only after it is complete should you choose tasks from work, school, home, or a community activity.

sections.title: Independent check: triage a changed case before seeing the key
paragraphs: Work independently on this changed-input case before reading the worked key. A school district receives photographs of damaged classroom equipment through a staff portal. Inputs are a photograph, room number, equipment ID, a short description, and a maintenance schedule. Objective: suggest whether the item appears unsafe, identify the equipment category, and place a proposed work order in a maintenance queue. Capability: image interpretation, classification, and text extraction. People: students, teachers, custodians, maintenance workers, and visitors. Consequence: a missed hazard could injure someone; an incorrectly urgent label could delay another repair, but a maintenance supervisor can inspect the item.

The system may read the submitted photograph and description and create a proposed work order. It may not declare a room safe, close a work order, send a student-facing message, or authorize a repair. A supervisor can edit or delete the proposal. The portal records the image, model result, supervisor correction, and final status. However, some photographs are blurry, equipment IDs may be missing, and the system has not yet been evaluated on different lighting conditions.

Write your release mode, verification method, stop condition, accountable owner, and correction or appeal path. Then explain whether the system should act on its own. Do not use the answer key yet. Ask: what evidence is incomplete, what permissions are necessary, what action is reversible, and who is exposed to the consequence of a missed hazard?
sections.callout: Independent attempt first: a plausible answer is not enough. Tie every control to an input, permission, consequence, or observable failure condition.

sections.title: Graduated hints for the changed case
paragraphs: Hint one: distinguish identifying a possible hazard from declaring a room safe. The former can be a reviewed proposal; the latter is a consequential action that needs stronger evidence and authority.
Hint two: blurry images and missing equipment IDs are incomplete evidence. A stop condition can route those cases to manual inspection rather than forcing a prediction.

Hint three: the maintenance supervisor is the accountable owner for accepting, correcting, or rejecting a proposed work order. Affected staff and students need a way to report that the description, location, or priority is wrong.

Hint four: permissions should allow a separate proposed work order but should not allow the system to close a work order, declare safety, or communicate a final decision. Verification should compare the image and description with a physical inspection.
sections.callout: Hints identify the reasoning steps without supplying the release mode.

sections.title: Key and feedback for the changed case
paragraphs: A justified first release is AI assistance with review. The system may propose a hazard flag, equipment category, and work-order draft, but a maintenance supervisor must inspect the item and approve the final work order. Do not choose automation with monitoring for the case as written. The evidence is incomplete because photographs can be blurry, equipment IDs can be missing, and evaluation across lighting conditions is not established. The consequence of missing a hazard is physical injury, while the draft remains reversible before dispatch.

Verification is a physical inspection that compares the photograph, room number, equipment ID when available, and description with the actual item. The supervisor confirms the hazard level and work-order details. Route a case to manual handling when the image is blurry, the room or equipment cannot be identified, the image and description conflict, or inspection shows that the proposed category or hazard level is unreliable. The accountable owner is the maintenance supervisor or district maintenance organization. The correction path lets staff report an incorrect room, equipment identity, hazard label, or work-order status and preserves the correction in the record.

No AI is also valid on the facts as written if the district finds no demonstrated benefit, prefers a manual baseline, or cannot justify the complete system's data use, permissions, review capacity, and expected benefit. AI assistance with review is currently justified because the supervisor inspects the item and approves the final work order. Limited automation with approval could become valid only if additional facts or evidence are established, such as documented evaluation, clear approval gates, and reliable handling of incomplete inputs. Automation with monitoring is not justified because the system would act without physical inspection even though a missed hazard can injure people. AI assistance without specified review, ownership, or verification is not a control. An alternative answer must distinguish these currently justified choices from a higher-authority mode that requires changed facts.
sections.callout: The strongest answer explains not only what to choose, but why the other choices are unsafe or what new facts would make them valid.

sections.title: Use the rubric, then choose your own tasks
paragraphs: Use this five-part rubric for both the supplied exercise and your own four tasks. Outcome and capability: identify a specific objective and a capability that fits it. Evidence and people: name the actual inputs or artifacts and the affected people. Consequence and mode: connect the likely harm and reversibility to a release mode. Controls: state permissions, verification, monitoring, and a stop or rollback condition. Accountability and remedy: name the owner and provide a correction, appeal, or escalation path where people may be affected.

A strong record is concrete, internally consistent, and tied to the case facts. A weak record says the model is accurate without naming a test, treats a model as the whole system, gives automation no permission boundary, or says a human is involved without specifying what that person verifies. A stop condition must be observable, such as an unreadable input, a failed comparison, a sensor outage, or a measured pattern of disagreement. A rollback condition must identify what can be undone and by whom.

Now choose four tasks from work, school, home, or a community activity and complete the original worksheet requirements. You may use text generation, summarization, explanation, format transformation, extraction, classification, brainstorming, image interpretation, audio transcription, ranking, recommendation, forecasting, or classical machine-learning pattern detection as capability examples. Optional names such as Meta Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Phi, Whisper, NVIDIA, and Z.ai are illustrative families only. The lesson makes no claim about their current features, ranking, or pricing. Provider name is not a substitute for evidence or controls.
sections.callout: A good use case has a clear outcome, suitable data, a quality check, and consequences that match the controls available.

activity.title: Triage four possible AI use cases
instructions: Choose four tasks from work, school, home, or a community activity.
For each task, identify the desired outcome, input data, AI capability, affected people, and consequence of a wrong result.
Classify the first release as no AI, AI assistance with review, limited automation with approval, or automation with monitoring.
Write one verification method and one stop or rollback condition for each task.

Before choosing your own tasks, complete the supplied food-pantry intake case using the dossier labels: objective, actual input or artifact, capability, affected people, consequence, permissions, reversibility, monitoring, release mode, verification, stop condition, accountable owner, and correction or appeal path.
For each of your four chosen tasks, add permissions, reversibility, monitoring, an accountable owner, and a correction or appeal path where people may be affected.
After your independent changed-input attempt, compare it with the key and explain which case facts justified the release mode.
evidence: A four-row use-case table containing outcome, data, capability, people, consequence, release mode, verification, and stop condition.
A short explanation of why the highest-risk task receives the strongest human control.
A completed offline record for the supplied food-pantry case and a separate independent record for the changed-input school-maintenance case.
A brief comparison identifying one incorrect alternative and the changed facts that could make it valid.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which task looked easy until you considered the complete system and the consequence of being wrong?

cues.text: Begin with the system view. Artificial intelligence is a broad term for computer systems performing tasks associated with perception, prediction, language, planning, or decision support. Machine learning is one way to create such behavior: it learns patterns from examples rather than requiring every rule to be written by hand. A model is only one component. The complete system also includes instructions, input data, software, tools, permissions, user experience, monitoring, and people who remain accountable. When you evaluate a product, ask what information enters it, what it can do, what it is allowed to change, and who checks the result.
Reveal a model in the center, then add input data, application code, tools, permissions, monitoring, users, and an accountable owner.
cues.accessibilityAlternative: A text list explains that an AI system contains a model plus data, application code, tools, permissions, monitoring, users, and an accountable owner. Reduced-motion mode displays all labels at once.

cues.text: Capability names help you match a method to a task, but they do not establish reliability. Generative systems can draft, summarize, explain, transform supplied material, extract structure, classify examples, brainstorm alternatives, or reason over material supplied in context. Other systems can rank, recommend, detect patterns, forecast values, transcribe audio, interpret images, or control physical processes. Start with the desired outcome and the available evidence. Ask whether the input is suitable, how quality will be checked, who is affected, and what happens if the result is wrong. NIST's Generative AI Profile is a risk-management companion, not a general capability catalog. Its citation here does not turn a capability list into a safety guarantee.
Practice pause: name one task where transforming supplied material is more appropriate than asking for an unsupported factual answer. State what source material a person would verify.

Assistance proposes work for a person to inspect. Automation may act without a person reviewing every output. Compare a private draft with an agent that sends a message, changes a record, dispatches a crew, or controls equipment. The model could be identical, but the permissions and consequences are not. Begin with assistance when the task is unfamiliar, evidence is incomplete, or mistakes are costly. Increase automation only after evaluation shows dependable behavior and the surrounding system can limit, observe, and reverse actions. No AI is also a valid first release when there is no demonstrated benefit or when a manual baseline is better.

Check your understanding: explain why the same model requires different controls when it moves from proposing a private draft to acting on a record or physical process. Name the permission, review, or rollback difference.

People and organizations choose the objective, acceptable risk, data, model, tools, evaluation method, permissions, and response when something goes wrong. An output can inform a decision, but it cannot accept responsibility for that decision. High-impact uses need clear ownership, meaningful review, correction or appeal paths, and evidence that the process performs acceptably for the people and situations it affects. A human name alone is not enough. The owner must have authority, time, information, and a defined action to take when evidence is missing or the result is wrong.

Introduce the dossier as a completed example. The library system creates a private announcement draft from a supplied brief, and the librarian checks every factual field before publication. The food-pantry system suggests a slot or missing field, but staff review every suggestion and the system cannot deny service or contact an applicant. The pothole system ranks reports for inspection, while an inspector retains approval authority for dispatch. The greenhouse system proposes an irrigation schedule, but a worker reviews it and can use a manual procedure. Notice that the cases do not need one of each mode. The modes follow evidence, permissions, reversibility, and consequences. A ranking method does not automatically justify automation, and a useful draft does not automatically justify publication.

Show four labelled case cards: library drafting, food-pantry intake, pothole ranking, and greenhouse irrigation. Each card lists input, objective, capability, people, consequence, permissions, verification, and stop condition.
cues.accessibilityAlternative: A static text list presents the four case cards and, for each, its input, objective, capability, affected people, consequence, permissions, verification, and stop condition. No animation is required.

cues.text: Trace the food-pantry case slowly. The scan and appointment data are inputs. Extraction and classification are model capabilities. The application places a suggestion in a staff queue. That queue, its permissions, review procedure, and logs are part of the complete system. A suggestion is not a fact and is not a decision. Staff compare it with the original form, correct it, and decide what happens next. The pantry organization remains accountable. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework describes AI systems as sociotechnical systems, so judge data, tools, people, controls, and the model together. NIST's Generative AI Profile is a risk-management companion, not a capability catalog. Sources are https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-1 and https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1. Ask learners to notice the boundary between proposing a result and taking action. Here the system may propose a staff task, but it may not deny service, alter the applicant record, or send a message. A correction and appeal path make accountability usable.

Practice pause: point to the exact step where the model produces an output, the step where the application presents it, and the step where an accountable person makes the decision. Then name one correction the applicant could request.

Now pause for the supplied onramp. Do not choose your own tasks yet. Use the food-pantry case and write one offline record. Include a concrete objective, the actual scan and appointment artifacts, a capability, affected people, consequence of error, permissions, reversibility, monitoring, release mode, verification, stop condition, owner, and correction or appeal path. Choose no AI if that is the most justified baseline. Otherwise justify the selected mode from the case facts. This is a conceptual exercise. No Python, deployment lab, or runnable code is needed. The purpose is to practice reasoning about a complete system.

Practice pause: complete the food-pantry record now. Before continuing, check that your stop condition is observable, your verification names what staff compare, and your release mode reflects what the system is actually permitted to do.

Next, work independently on the changed school-maintenance case before reading the key. The system receives a photograph, room number, equipment ID, and description. It may propose a hazard flag, category, and work-order draft, but it cannot declare a room safe, close a work order, or send a final message. The important facts are the physical consequence of a missed hazard, the supervisor's approval, the ability to correct a draft, and incomplete evidence from blurry photographs, missing IDs, and unevaluated lighting conditions. Write the release mode, verification, stop condition, owner, and remedy. Do not choose an answer merely because the model sounds confident. No AI remains available if the district does not find a demonstrated benefit or cannot justify safe review and data handling.

Practice pause: make your independent choice before opening the hints or key. Explain what the system may do, what it may not do, what evidence would cause a manual handoff, and why no AI might or might not be the best baseline.

Offer the hints one at a time. First, distinguish a possible hazard flag from a declaration that a room is safe. Second, treat a blurry image or missing identifier as incomplete evidence, not as permission to guess. Third, name the maintenance supervisor as accountable owner and provide a way to correct the location, identity, hazard label, or status. Fourth, keep the permission boundary at a separate proposed work order and require physical inspection before final action. These hints support reasoning, but they do not force adoption of AI. A manual route can be the right answer when the expected benefit has not been demonstrated.

Give the worked key only after the independent attempt. Assistance with review is justified by the case as written: the supervisor inspects the item and approves the final work order. Automation with monitoring is not justified because a missed hazard can injure someone and the evidence is incomplete. Verification compares the image, room, identifier, and description with the physical item. The stop condition routes cases to manual handling when the image is blurry, the location is uncertain, fields conflict, or inspection shows unreliable categorization. No AI is also valid if the district finds no demonstrated benefit, prefers a manual baseline, or cannot provide justified review and data controls. Limited automation could become valid after documented evaluation, approval gates, and safe handling of incomplete inputs. The answer is conditional reasoning, not memorizing a mode.

Close with the rubric. A strong record has a specific outcome, fitting capability, actual inputs or artifacts, affected people, consequence, release mode, permissions, reversibility, monitoring, verification, stop or rollback condition, accountable owner, and remedy. Weak records say accurate without naming a test, call the model the whole system, give automation no permission boundary, or mention human involvement without naming what the person checks. Now choose four tasks from your own context. Consider text, vision, audio, ranking, recommendation, forecasting, or pattern detection. Provider names do not establish current features, ranking, price, or benefit. For every task, compare AI with a manual or no-AI baseline and adopt AI only when the complete system has a demonstrated, justified benefit.

Practice pause: for each of your four tasks, underline the consequence, circle the accountable owner, and draw an arrow from the verification step to the stop or rollback condition. Then write one sentence explaining why your selected mode is better justified than no AI, or why no AI is the appropriate baseline.

Guide the learner through the four-use-case triage table and ask them to defend the strongest control. For each task, require the outcome, input data, capability, affected people, consequence, release mode, verification, and stop or rollback condition. Remind learners that no AI is a valid option and that a mode must follow actual authority, evidence, reversibility, and consequences.

Invite the learner to complete the knowledge check only after the table includes verification and a stop condition. Ask the learner to explain why the selected mode follows the permissions and consequences, and to identify when a manual or no-AI baseline would be more justified.

Timing note: the narration contains 1,247 words. At an assumed 120 words per minute, spoken narration takes about 10.4 minutes. A roughly 24-minute session can allocate 10.4 minutes to narration, 4 minutes to the supplied food-pantry practice, 3 minutes to the changed school case, 3.6 minutes to your own four tasks, and 3 minutes to assessment and reflection. These are planning values, not a guarantee. Pause longer for writing, replay sections, or take optional extended time. Quality of reasoning matters more than finishing on this estimate.

captions.text: Begin with the system view. Artificial intelligence is a broad term for computer systems performing tasks associated with perception, prediction, language, planning, or decision support. Machine learning is one way to create such behavior: it learns patterns from examples rather than requiring every rule to be written by hand. A model is only one component. The complete system also includes instructions, input data, software, tools, permissions, user experience, monitoring, and people who remain accountable. When you evaluate a product, ask what information enters it, what it can do, what it is allowed to change, and who checks the result.

Capability names help you match a method to a task, but they do not establish reliability. Generative systems can draft, summarize, explain, transform supplied material, extract structure, classify examples, brainstorm alternatives, or reason over material supplied in context. Other systems can rank, recommend, detect patterns, forecast values, transcribe audio, interpret images, or control physical processes. Start with the desired outcome and the available evidence. Ask whether the input is suitable, how quality will be checked, who is affected, and what happens if the result is wrong. NIST's Generative AI Profile is a risk-management companion, not a general capability catalog. Its citation here does not turn a capability list into a safety guarantee.

Assistance proposes work for a person to inspect. Automation may act without a person reviewing every output. Compare a private draft with an agent that sends a message, changes a record, dispatches a crew, or controls equipment. The model could be identical, but the permissions and consequences are not. Begin with assistance when the task is unfamiliar, evidence is incomplete, or mistakes are costly. Increase automation only after evaluation shows dependable behavior and the surrounding system can limit, observe, and reverse actions. No AI is also a valid first release when there is no demonstrated benefit or when a manual baseline is better.

People and organizations choose the objective, acceptable risk, data, model, tools, evaluation method, permissions, and response when something goes wrong. An output can inform a decision, but it cannot accept responsibility for that decision. High-impact uses need clear ownership, meaningful review, correction or appeal paths, and evidence that the process performs acceptably for the people and situations it affects. A human name alone is not enough. The owner must have authority, time, information, and a defined action to take when evidence is missing or the result is wrong.

Introduce the dossier as a completed example. The library system creates a private announcement draft from a supplied brief, and the librarian checks every factual field before publication. The food-pantry system suggests a slot or missing field, but staff review every suggestion and the system cannot deny service or contact an applicant. The pothole system ranks reports for inspection, while an inspector retains approval authority for dispatch. The greenhouse system proposes an irrigation schedule, but a worker reviews it and can use a manual procedure. Notice that the cases do not need one of each mode. The modes follow evidence, permissions, reversibility, and consequences. A ranking method does not automatically justify automation, and a useful draft does not automatically justify publication.

Trace the food-pantry case slowly. The scan and appointment data are inputs. Extraction and classification are model capabilities. The application places a suggestion in a staff queue. That queue, its permissions, review procedure, and logs are part of the complete system. A suggestion is not a fact and is not a decision. Staff compare it with the original form, correct it, and decide what happens next. The pantry organization remains accountable. instructorScript.reducedMotionAlternative: Display all visual information as static labelled text. The system diagram lists model, input data, application software, tools, permissions, monitoring, users, and accountable owner. The dossier lists the four cases and their controls. No reveals, transitions, animated arrows, or timed visual changes are required. questions.prompt: Which description best represents a complete AI system?
choices: A model by itself
A model combined with data, software, tools, controls, users, and accountable people
Any application that produces text
A database containing every correct answer
questions.explanation: The behavior and risk come from the complete system, not from the model alone.

questions.prompt: Which task is generally the strongest starting point for AI assistance?
choices: Automatically approve a high-impact benefit decision
Draft three alternatives from supplied material for a person to review
Delete production records when a response sounds confident
Provide an uncited medical diagnosis
questions.explanation: Drafting alternatives from supplied material has a clear review step and avoids irreversible action.

questions.prompt: What changes most when a workflow moves from assistance to automation?
choices: The spelling of the prompt
The system may act without a person reviewing every output
The model becomes a database
Verification is no longer necessary
questions.explanation: Automation changes who or what acts and therefore increases the importance of permissions, monitoring, and recovery.

questions.prompt: Who remains accountable for selecting and operating an AI-supported process?
choices: The model
The training dataset
The people and organization deploying the system
No one when the output is generated automatically
questions.explanation: People and organizations choose the purpose, controls, and response to harm; the model cannot accept accountability.

questions.prompt: Which set of questions is most useful when evaluating an AI use case?
choices: Is it popular, fast, and visually impressive?
What is the outcome, what data is used, who is affected, what happens if it is wrong, and how is it verified?
Can it remove every human from the process?
Does the product use the largest available model?
questions.explanation: Outcome, data, affected people, consequences, and verification expose whether the complete use case is appropriate.
